report:
### Conclusion
Scientific evidence generally supports the claim that chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation reduces surgical-site infection (SSI) risk following cesarean delivery compared to iodine-based preparations, though some trials report non-significant differences depending on the specific iodine formulation used.

### Evidence
* **Primary Evidence Supporting Chlorhexidine-Alcohol:** A landmark randomized controlled trial published in *The New England Journal of Medicine* directly compared chlorhexidine-alcohol to iodine-alcohol for preoperative skin preparation prior to cesarean delivery. It found a significantly lower SSI rate in the chlorhexidine-alcohol group compared with the iodine-alcohol group (4.0% vs. 7.3%; relative risk 0.55) (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048).
* **Systematic Reviews:** A Cochrane review concluded that preparing the skin with chlorhexidine gluconate before a cesarean section is likely more effective at reducing post-cesarean SSIs than povidone-iodine (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007462_skin-preparation-preventing-infection-following-caesarean-section). Additionally, a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials found that alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine had the highest probability of preventing SSIs among evaluated antiseptics (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282).
* **Counter-Evidence & Nuance:** Some studies found less pronounced differences. The CAPICA trial compared chlorhexidine-alcohol to an aqueous povidone-iodine scrub-and-paint preparation and found no statistically significant difference in SSI rates between the two groups (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/).

Overall, while certain trial comparisons show similar efficacy, high-quality evidence and meta-analyses favor alcohol-based chlorhexidine over iodine preparations for post-cesarean SSI prevention.
